Just a thought: since you don't know German anyway, consider going to school in the French-speaking part of the country. A city known for its international organizations and another city nearby have excellent schools.

The challenge with a major city in the central part of the country is that you'll have to learn not one but two languages: German and a local dialect. The latter is a set of dialects spread throughout the region and is the everyday language, while German is the official language. You can learn German, and speakers of the local dialect can all speak German, but knowing German won't help you understand much of the local dialect; everyday life is a little tougher if you don't know it. It's also largely useless outside of the country.

On the flip side, I would imagine that classes in the major city are taught in German, so you'll have that going for you.

However, since you're from Canada, learning French will probably come in handy, rather than German or Italian. The French spoken in the country is not quite the same as the one spoken in Quebec, but it's easy to get used to one if you know the other. Canadian French has a very characteristic set of dialects that -- when compared to standard French -- feature big differences in pronunciation, small differences in vocabulary, and the same grammar. Swiss French is essentially the same as the French spoken in France, with a mild accent and a few particularities in vocabulary. I'd say the differences are similar to those you'd encounter as a Canadian traveling to the British Isles.

So in other words, since you'll have to learn a language anyway, you might as well learn one that you're more likely to use back home. Certainly, it never hurts to know German, though it's less likely to be useful. The francophone world is quite large, between Canada, Europe, parts of the Caribbean, Africa, or even Polynesia.

On the plus side, topics like political science and economics often feature some classes in English.

The smaller city is a quaint place nestled by a lake in a beautiful valley, and there's no place like that region elsewhere on Earth.

People in the United States can't just "take you in" and help you find a job. You're not authorized to stay in the long term: 3 months at a time at the most if you're from a visa waiver program country, otherwise you need to apply for a tourist visa (which are valid from 1 to 10 years and allow you to visit up to 6 months at a time). You're also not legally allowed to work in the US (just like I probably would not be allowed to work in your country without a work visa).

So you need a work visa. To get a work visa, you need to find a job in the US with an employer who is willing to sponsor you for a work visa. That employer will then file paperwork with the US immigration administration so you can then apply for a visa with your local US embassy. You'd have to have in-demand professional qualifications in order to obtain a work visa.

Of course, you could also get a student visa and come study in the US, or an exchange visa and come to the US for a limited time, for something like a cultural exchange, summer camp, stuff like that.

None of these things will ever allow you to become a US citizen, however. The first and main requirement to applying for naturalization is to be a permanent resident for a number of years, a.k.a. a green card holder. It's possible to become a permanent resident through employment, although, again, you'd have to be a qualified professional in a given field in order to have a chance. By far the easiest way to get a green card is to marry a US citizen. There's also the annual green card lottery.

You can solve this easily by removing port 22 from the security group and re-adding it with more specific source IP addresses than all IP addresses, assuming you know where connections will be coming from.

If you want to set up a VPN, then yes, you'll need to implement something like OpenVPN to serve VPN clients. OpenVPN can run on the same server as your web application if you prefer, or you can establish a brand new server dedicated to running OpenVPN. Then you configure your security group to accept connections on port 22 only from the subnet that OpenVPN assigns to clients, allowing VPN users to connect to your web server.

So if the subnet you set up for OpenVPN's DHCP is, for example, 10.10.0.0/24, the security group assigned to your web server will look like this:

- All IP addresses (anywhere) -> TCP 80 = allow
- All IP addresses (anywhere) -> TCP 443 = allow
- 10.10.0.0/24 -> TCP 22 = allow

The easiest way is for you two to get married. There are two main types of visas for that: one where you're not married, go to the US and get married, and one where you're already married and apply to immigrate to the US.

The former is known as a fiancé visa, category K-1. Basically, she has to ask for one on your behalf. If approved, the petition is forwarded to your local US embassy, you apply for the visa there and, if accepted, you get to go to the US under a special nonimmigrant status whose expressed purpose is to allow you to apply for what's called adjustment of status, whereby you request to have your nonimmigrant status adjusted to an immigrant status, in this case a legal permanent resident, a.k.a. LPR, a.k.a. green card holder. Once you're in the US, you two have to get married within 90 days and apply for adjustment of status, or you have to leave the US. So this is a good opportunity to make sure you want to get married.

If you're already married, it's a similar process but the visa category is CR-1. It can also be IR-1 if you've been married for more than 2 years, but that wouldn't apply to you at this time. So, again, your spouse would have to file a petition with the immigration service, if approved it's sent to your local US embassy, then you apply for the visa there, if approved you get to go to the US and you immediately become a legal permanent resident upon arrival and admittance into the country. You'll get your actual green card in the mail a few weeks later.

I could tell you all about it but the nice people at the site wrote it all down in nice, convenient guides so I don't have to reinvent the wheel :) Also check out their forums if you like, but you don't need to.

For a K-1, the initial cost for the main form your girlfriend has to file is $535 -- see details and the form itself on the immigration service's website. There may be other fees associated with applying for the visa at the embassy, and various, small expenses related to obtaining all the paperwork you'll have to assemble. And you'll have to have a medical exam, I don't know how much that would cost under the national health system.

Once you're in the US and once you're married (again -- within 90 days of your arrival), you will need to file a new form for adjustment of status, the cost of which is currently $1,225 for most applicants. This gets you your green card, once it's approved.

Optionally (but recommended), at the same time you file for adjustment of status, you can also file for work authorization and a travel document. Those two normally carry a fee, but are free when filed alongside the adjustment of status application.

The work authorization application allows you to work legally in the US. They're usually approved faster than green cards so if you need money, it's a good idea, and since it's free anyway, you might as well.

The travel document application allows you to depart the US and come back before you have your green card. This is useful in case something happens back home and compels you to go in person. If you don't have a travel document and don't have your green card yet, you will not be admissible into the US.

The initial cost for the CR-1 visa is $535 currently, and again there may be various fees associated with gathering paperwork for your application for the visa at the US embassy. Since you'll become a legal permanent resident upon arrival in the US, there are no more forms to file at that time.

Either way, your significant other will also have to meet certain income requirements. This is to ensure you do not become a burden of the state once you're in the US. They're not difficult requirements to meet but if you're young, e.g. in school, and have no steady income, it can be an obstacle. In the eyes of the government, she will be financially responsible for you for 10 years or until you become a US citizen.

The K-1 or CR-1 process takes several months, and if you do a K-1, the green card process will take several additional months after you arrive in the US.

Once you're in the US and have your green card, you shouldn't need to talk to the government for about two years.

Take advantage of public transportation! The Swiss railways are famous, and the local network is pretty good. Don't own a car unless you need one, and consider carefully and objectively whether you need one. Your American mindset will try to sway you (unless you're from a major city with good public transport -- then you should fit right in), but consider that you can get to a lot of places on foot in the city. Biking is also popular.

Be careful of pickpockets whenever you're out in public, on or off public transportation. It won't be long until you see people begging on the street; it's up to you whether to give them money, but be aware that a lot of them are organized groups, and the money you give often doesn't go to the person you see on the street, even when they're with a small child. Some of them also organize confidence schemes (and are incredibly good at packing up and vanishing at the first sight of law enforcement), so don't fall for it. Actual homeless people are not all that common, but you can easily tell them apart from the others.

If you're going to live in Switzerland, you must have healthcare; it's the law. It's all provided by private companies, and you pick everything depending on how much you want to spend vs. what coverage you want. There's a minimum standard of coverage every insurance provides that cannot be denied to you regardless of any pre-existing conditions. Some employers may provide you with health coverage, but for most people, the premiums are 100% out of pocket. We do OK though.

If you're going to work in Switzerland, you'll have to pay taxes to the federal government as well as to your canton of residence. Switzerland is like the US in that it's also a federation of states, which we call cantons. In the US, though, you can get your employer to take out your taxes from your paycheck automatically. And there's a catch with taxes, at least in the city I mentioned: your yearly income puts you in one or the other tax bracket, and that determines your tax liability -- not what you actually earned. In other words, if your yearly salary is 100,000 but you arrive in the middle of the year and only actually receive 50,000, you'll be in a different tax bracket (and will owe more) than if your yearly salary was 50,000 and you had been there the whole year and actually earned the full 50,000.

And don't forget that as a US citizen, you must file a federal tax return with the IRS even if you live abroad, but you only owe taxes on what you make above a certain amount to the tune of $90-something-thousand, and you can usually negate part of it with what you paid to Switzerland.
